items.title: Belts double your survival chances
items.simple: Wear your seat belt. It can double your chance of living through a crash. It can more than double your chance of avoiding a bad injury.
items.official: Wearing seat belts, also called safety belts, can double your chances of surviving a crash and more than double your chances of avoiding serious injury.
items.mnemonic: Buckle once, double your chances.

items.title: Everyone buckles, front and back
items.simple: In Virginia, everyone in the car must wear a seat belt. That means the driver and every passenger, in the front seat and the back seat.
items.official: Under Virginia law, the driver and all passengers, both front and rear, must wear safety belts.
items.mnemonic: Every seat, every trip.

items.title: Driver secures riders under 18
items.simple: If you drive anyone under 18, you must make sure that person is buckled in. That means a seat belt, a booster seat or a child seat. This is true in every seat.
items.official: A driver transporting anyone younger than age 18 must ensure that the passenger is properly secured in a safety belt, booster seat or child safety seat no matter where the child is seated in the vehicle.
items.mnemonic: Rider under 18? The driver checks the buckle.

items.title: Lap belt low and snug
items.simple: Wear the lap belt low on your lap, against your thighs. Your lap belt and shoulder belt should both be snug, not loose.
items.official: Remember to wear your lap belt low on your lap and against your thighs. Your shoulder and lap belts should be snug.
items.mnemonic: Low and snug, like a hug.

items.title: Shoulder belt across your chest
items.simple: Wear the shoulder belt over your shoulder and across your chest. Never put it behind your back. Never put it under your arm.
items.official: Wear your shoulder belt over your shoulder and across your chest. Never wear your shoulder belt behind your back or under your arm.
items.mnemonic: Over and across. Never behind, never under.

items.title: Pregnant: belt low on pelvis
items.simple: If you are pregnant, you are much safer buckled up. Wear the belt as low on your pelvis (hip bones) as you can.
items.official: Pregnant women are much safer if buckled up by wearing the belt as low on the pelvis as possible.
items.mnemonic: Baby on board? The belt rides low.

items.title: Doctor's seat belt waiver
items.simple: A doctor can excuse you from wearing a seat belt if there is a physical or medical reason. You must then carry the doctor's signed note. The note names you and the reason.
items.official: A waiver of the seat belt requirement may be granted by a licensed physician if the use of a safety belt is not reasonable due to the driver's or passenger's physical or medical condition. The person granted the waiver must carry the physician's signed written statement identifying the person with the waiver and the reason for the waiver.
items.mnemonic: Doctor's excuse? Carry the note.

items.title: Air bags work with belts
items.simple: Air bags work with seat belts, not instead of them. In a front crash, the air bag cushions you. It keeps your head, neck and chest from hitting the steering wheel or dashboard. Always buckle up.
items.official: Air bags, when used properly with safety belts, cushion drivers and passengers as they move forward in a front-end crash. By providing a cushion, the air bag keeps the head, neck and chest from hitting the steering column or dashboard, and reduces the force of impact. Always buckle up and have all passengers in the vehicle buckle up.
items.mnemonic: Bag plus belt = a team. Always click it.

items.title: Sit 10 inches from wheel
items.simple: If your car has air bags, move your seat back. Sit at least 10 inches from the steering wheel.
items.official: Move your seat back so that you are at least ten inches from the steering wheel.
items.mnemonic: Ten fingers, ten inches.

items.title: Tilt steering wheel down
items.simple: If your steering wheel can tilt, tilt it down. Then the air bag points at your chest, not your head and neck.
items.official: If your steering wheel is adjustable, tilt it downward. This points the air bag toward your chest instead of your head and neck.
items.mnemonic: Tilt down, aim at the chest.

items.title: Kids 12 and under: back seat
items.simple: If your car has air bags, kids age 12 and under are safer buckled up in the back seat.
items.official: Children ages 12 and under are safer buckled up in the back seat.
items.mnemonic: 12 and under? Back seat buddy.

items.title: Under 8: child or booster seat
items.simple: All kids under 8 must ride in a child safety seat or booster seat. This is the law.
items.official: All children under age 8 must be properly secured in a child safety seat or booster seat when riding in vehicles manufactured after January 1, 1968.
items.mnemonic: Kid number ladder: 2 face back, 8 booster, 12 back seat, 16 no truck bed.

items.title: Rear facing until age 2
items.simple: Children should ride facing the back of the car from birth to age 2. They can ride that way longer if the car seat maker allows it.
items.official: Children should ride rear facing from birth to 2 years, or as long as the safety seat manufacturer allows.
items.mnemonic: Birth to 2? Face the back, too.

items.title: Rear-facing seat in front: rare
items.simple: If your car has no back seat, a rear-facing child seat may go in the front passenger seat. The car must have no passenger air bag, or the air bag must be turned off.
items.official: If the vehicle does not have a back seat, a rear facing child seat may be placed in the front passenger seat if the vehicle is not equipped with a passenger side air bag or if the passenger air bag is turned off.
items.mnemonic: Baby seat up front? Air bag off.

items.title: Forward facing seat until 8
items.simple: After the rear-facing stage, kids ride facing forward in a child safety seat or booster seat. Keep them there until at least age 8, or until the seat belt fits them properly.
items.official: Children should ride facing forward in a child safety seat or booster seat until at least age 8, or until they can attain a proper seat belt fit.
items.mnemonic: Face back to 2. Face forward to 8.

items.title: No booster: belt must fit
items.simple: A child can stop using a booster only when the belt fits. The lap belt lies snugly across the upper thighs. The shoulder belt lies snugly across the shoulder and chest.
items.official: Criteria for sitting without a booster seat: Lap belt lies snugly across the upper thighs. Shoulder belt lies snugly across the shoulder and chest.
items.mnemonic: Lap belt on thighs. Shoulder belt on chest.

items.title: No booster: sitting checklist
items.simple: To ride without a booster, a child must sit properly for the whole trip. That means sitting tall without slouching, all the way back against the seat, with knees bent over the seat edge and feet flat on the floor.
items.official: Criteria for sitting without a booster seat: Tall enough to sit without slouching. Able to keep knees naturally bent over the edge of the vehicle seat. Able to sit all the way back against the vehicle seat back. Able to keep feet flat on the floor. Able to sit this way for entire trip.
items.mnemonic: Back in, knees bent, feet flat, sit tall, whole trip.

items.title: Doctor's child seat waiver
items.simple: A doctor can excuse a child from the child seat law. The reason can be the child's weight, fitness or another medical reason. The person driving the child must carry the doctor's signed note.
items.official: A waiver of the child restraint law may be granted by a licensed physician if using a child restraint would be unreasonable due to the child's weight, physical fitness or other medical reasons. The person responsible for transporting this child must carry the signed written statement by the physician identifying the child and stating the grounds for the waiver.
items.mnemonic: The doctor's note rides with the child.

items.title: Child seat fines: $50, $500
items.simple: The driver must make sure kids are buckled in correctly. If you break the child seat law, you pay a $50 fine. A second offense can cost $500.
items.official: The driver is responsible for making sure that children are properly secured. If you are convicted of violating the child restraint law, you will be fined $50. A second or subsequent offense could mean a $500 penalty.
items.mnemonic: First $50, then add a zero: $500.

items.title: Center back seat is safest
items.simple: The safest spot for a child safety seat is the middle of the back seat. Many places in Virginia hold car seat checks. Go to one to make sure your seat is installed correctly.
items.official: The safest place to install a child safety seat is in the center of the back seat. Numerous child safety seat checks are held in localities across Virginia. Attend one of these checks to make sure that your child's safety seat is installed correctly.
items.mnemonic: Middle of the back is the safest track.

items.title: Never hold a child in lap
items.simple: Never hold a child on your lap in a car. In a crash, the child can get crushed between you and the dashboard or the back of the seat.
items.official: Never hold a child in your lap. In a crash, the child may be crushed between your body and the dashboard or the back of the seat.
items.mnemonic: Laps are for story time, not drive time.

items.title: Lock doors, use child locks
items.simple: Close and lock all doors before you drive. Turn on the child safety lock if you have one. Don't let kids play with door handles. If you must open a door, pull off the road and stop.
items.official: Make sure that all car doors are securely closed and locked before driving. If your car is equipped with a child safety lock, turn it on. Don't allow children to play with door handles or locks. If you must open a door, pull the vehicle off the road and come to a complete stop.
items.mnemonic: Lock it before you roll. Stop before you open.

items.title: No kids in luggage area
items.simple: Never let kids ride in the luggage area of a hatchback, station wagon or van. Never leave a hatchback open when a child rides in the back seat.
items.official: Never allow children to ride in the luggage area of hatchbacks, station wagons or vans. Never leave a hatchback open when a child is riding in the back seat.
items.mnemonic: Bags ride in the back. Kids ride in seats.

items.title: Under 16: no pickup bed
items.simple: Never carry kids under 16 in the bed of a pickup truck. It is against the law. A camper shell on top does not make it legal.
items.official: It is illegal to transport children under age 16 in the bed of a pickup truck, even if equipped with a camper shell.
items.mnemonic: Under 16? Cab, not bed.

items.title: Correct child seats save lives
items.simple: Install the child seat correctly. A correctly installed seat can greatly lower a child's chance of death or injury in a crash.
items.official: Securing a child in a correctly installed child safety seat can significantly reduce the possibility of death or injury.

items.title: Air bag on/off switch: ask NHTSA
items.simple: To learn more about air bags, or to apply for an air bag on-off switch, contact NHTSA. That is the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration.
items.official: For more information about air bags, including applying for an on/off switch, contact the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA).
